documents.title: Academic Integrity Guidelines for AI Use
documents.summary: Landing page stating Texas State has no university AI policy, leaving AI rules to instructors, and pointing to student and faculty guidelines and other offices.
documents.stance_why: The page says the university has no AI policy and that instructors have 'academic freedom to determine appropriate use for their own courses', so it sets no stance itself and hands the decision to instructors; no tiers are offered.

units.why: States that because there is 'no policy', each instructor decides what is appropriate in their own courses. This is a per-instructor decision rule, so P04; it takes no position on AI itself, hence neutral.
units.anchor: provides instructors the academic freedom to determine appropriate use for their own courses

units.why: Instructors are 'strongly encouraged' (a recommendation, so should) to state what is permissible regarding AI in their courses; this is the syllabus/assignment AI statement type P09.
units.anchor: strongly encouraged to outline their expectations
units.policy: Instructors are strongly encouraged to outline their expectations for completing assignments and provide explicit instructions on what is permissible regarding AI use.
units.fit_note: Strongly encouraged rather than required, and not limited to the syllabus.

units.why: Points instructors to Faculty Success resources and sample syllabus statements; this is support for faculty in handling AI, so P63, and it only informs.
units.anchor: guidance on how to talk to students about AI and examples of syllabus statements

documents.title: Student AI Guidelines
documents.summary: Student-facing Honor Code guidance: students must know each course's AI rules, remain responsible for submitted content, treat unauthorized AI use as existing misconduct, and take care with Grammarly, Copilot and Chrome extensions.
documents.stance_why: The guidelines make permissibility depend on the professor: 'If a professor has not permitted the use of AI tools' use may violate the Honor Code, and 'Whether this violates the Honor Code policy will depend on the professor's course policy'. The document sets no uniform stance and hands the decision to courses.

units.why: Students are 'expected to know' what each course allows; the duty is to learn the course rules, so P78 with must.
units.anchor: students at TXST are expected to know whether AI tools can be used

units.why: When the syllabus is silent, students are 'encouraged to ask' the professor; this is P10 (ask before using), not P06 because no fallback prohibition is stated.
units.anchor: students are encouraged to ask them directly whether AI tools can be used

units.why: States that students own what they submit: 'responsible for the content produced', so P29.
units.anchor: Students are responsible for the content produced for the course

units.why: Compares unauthorized AI use to help from another person or resource, i.e. AI is handled like a human collaborator under existing rules, P45.
units.anchor: Unauthorized AI use can be treated as analogous to assistance from another person or resource

units.why: Says existing Honor Code violations (cheating, plagiarism, fabrication) 'also extend' to AI materials, classifying unauthorized AI use as misconduct, P36.
units.anchor: also extend to using generated-AI materials or other AI-powered tools

units.why: The same sentence names browser extensions as AI tools covered by the Honor Code, which is the browser-embedded AI coverage of P07; kept separate from the P36 unit because it adds a distinct scope.
units.anchor: AI-powered tools like Chrome Extensions
units.policy: AI-powered tools like Chrome Extensions are covered by the existing Honor Code examples.
units.fit_note: P07 centers on editors, IDEs and agents; this is a browser extension scope statement without a rule to disable.

units.why: Students must follow the AI rules of each course or assignment; learning and following course rules is P78.
units.anchor: Students are responsible for following course- and/or assignment-specific AI policies

units.why: If AI is not permitted, using the generative function of Grammarly or Copilot to create part of a draft 'may violate' the Honor Code. This names embedded writing and coding assistants (P07), chosen over P19 because the passage is about those tools; also an unless-permitted fallback.
units.anchor: generative AI function in Grammarly or CoPilot to create part of a draft may violate
units.fit_note: Also states a default that unpermitted generative drafting may violate the Honor Code (P06/P19 content).

units.why: When AI use is allowed, students must follow disclosure requirements such as citation or addendum; this is P24 (disclose with the submission).
units.anchor: please make sure you follow any disclosure requirements (e.g., citation, addendum, etc.)

units.why: Students using Grammarly under a professor's AI ban must turn the generative function off; this is a require-to-disable rule for embedded AI, P07.
units.anchor: professor has banned the use of AI tools, please make sure you have
units.policy: If a professor has banned the use of AI tools, students who use Grammarly must turn the generative AI function off.

units.why: Treats Grammarly's reactive core tools (spelling, clarity, tone) as learning aids and not generative AI, exempting routine features from the AI rules, P100. This is inferred from 'typically viewed as learning aids'; it is not an explicit permission.
units.anchor: Grammarly’s core grammar and revision tools
units.policy: Grammarly's core grammar and revision tools (spelling, clarity, fluency, tone) are reactive and typically viewed as learning aids, distinct from generative AI.
units.fit_note: Framed as how the tools are 'typically viewed', not as an explicit exemption.

units.why: Defines what makes Grammarly's AI generative (generating or rephrasing content from prompts) so students can tell which function the rules cover; a definition of scope, P61.
units.anchor: can be used to generate or rephrase content using prompts

units.why: Warns that Grammarly's generative AI carries the same integrity risks as ChatGPT or Copilot. This treats it like other generative AI, closest to P36 (improper use is an integrity matter).
units.anchor: it still carries the same academic integrity risks as ChatGPT or Copilot
units.fit_note: A risk warning, not a classification of conduct as misconduct.

units.why: Tells students that platforms monitor Chrome extensions and professors may be notified, which is detection of misuse through tools, P40.
units.anchor: many platforms used by faculty are monitoring the use of Chrome extensions

units.why: Describes students pasting questions into AI or using extensions to answer them as a concern. It names the pasted-question behavior of P20 as a problem, informing rather than ruling.
units.anchor: copying/pasting questions into AI (such as ChatGPT) or by having an AI browser extension
units.fit_note: Describes a concern about the behavior; no explicit prohibition is stated.

units.why: Makes the violation question depend on the professor's course policy, a per-instructor rule, P04.
units.anchor: Whether this violates the Honor Code policy will depend on the professor’s course policy

documents.title: Faculty AI Guidelines
documents.summary: Faculty-facing Honor Code guidance: communicate a course AI statement and remind students, treat Turnitin AI scores as insufficient on their own, weigh signs of AI use, and guard against Chrome answer extensions with proctoring and HCC help.
documents.stance_why: The guidance only 'strongly encourage[s]' faculty to write AI usage statements and sets no stance on AI use itself; what counts as unauthorized is left to the course policy ('unauthorized or inappropriate resources').

units.why: Faculty 'should communicate' with students about AI; communicating course expectations is P09 (state AI expectations).
units.anchor: Faculty should communicate with their students about the use of AI in their courses
units.fit_note: Communication is advised generally, not specifically in the syllabus.

units.why: Recommends ('strongly encouraged') a syllabus AI usage statement, matching P09.
units.anchor: faculty are strongly encouraged to outline an AI usage statement in their syllabi

units.why: Asks faculty to repeat the AI policy during the term and before exams, i.e. more than listing the rule once. Nearest is P66 (explain and discuss the rules), though no explanation is required.
units.anchor: remind students of the course/assignment AI policy periodically throughout the course and before major exams
units.fit_note: Periodic reminders, not explanation or discussion of reasons.

units.why: Says Turnitin AI-writing reports can be useful but produce false positives and negatives, so detector reliability is limited; P39 is about not relying on detectors, which this supports without banning their use.
units.anchor: false positives and negatives do occur
units.fit_note: Detectors are described as useful but fallible rather than rejected.

units.why: A detector score 'cannot be the sole evidence' of misconduct: a standard for evidence in AI-misuse findings, P69.
units.anchor: the score cannot be the sole evidence of academic misconduct

units.why: Faculty should screen all assignments themselves whatever the report says, i.e. use their own checks as process evidence, P40.
units.anchor: professors should still screen all their assignments for signs of academic dishonesty
units.fit_note: Manual screening by the instructor, not a tool.

units.why: Lists a sign of possible dishonesty that instructors may weigh, a kind of evidence in AI-misuse findings, P69.
units.anchor: does not meet the assignment requirements or use concepts addressed within the course content

units.why: Another listed kind of evidence, obvious signs of AI use such as hallucinations; P69.
units.anchor: obvious signs of AI use (hallucinations, reference to the use of a large language model

units.why: Lists inconsistency with the student's other work as a sign of misuse to weigh as evidence, P69.
units.anchor: inconsistent with other work produced by the student

units.why: Points instructors who suspect unauthorized resource use to a blog on collecting evidence; guidance on how to gather evidence, nearest P69.
units.anchor: you may find this blog on
units.fit_note: Refers to outside guidance rather than stating an evidence standard.

units.why: Names Honor Code leadership as the office that supports faculty with suspected violations, P80 (who owns and enforces); it states no process.
units.anchor: Honor Code leadership is also here to help
units.fit_note: Names an office offering help, not an owner or exceptions process.

units.why: Recommends proctoring tools to guard against AI answer extensions in online assessments. It is tool-based detection or prevention, P40; P33 and P22 fit less since there is no stated shift in assessment weight or ban.
units.anchor: utilize proctoring tools like Proctorio, ProctorU, and TopHat
units.fit_note: Proctoring as prevention for online work, beyond similarity or process evidence.

units.why: States the Honor Code Council gets TopHat information on in-class, homework and unmonitored work, a tool-based way of identifying misuse, P40.
units.anchor: the HCC receives information from TopHat for in-class questions, homework assignments, or unmonitored tests

units.why: Instructors who suspect a Chrome extension should contact the Honor Code Council; a step in reporting suspected misuse, P81.
units.anchor: please contact the HCC to inquire about the potential use in your class
units.fit_note: An informal inquiry to the HCC, not a formal report.

documents.title: Guidelines for the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Tools
documents.summary: Information Security Office guidelines on AI tools for the whole community: protect confidential data, take responsibility for and review AI output, follow integrity rules set by instructors, and follow procurement processes. They are guidelines drawn from existing policy, not new policy.
documents.stance_why: The guidelines say they are 'not new University policy' and set no general stance on AI use in coursework; they leave permitted uses to instructors ('Faculty should be clear with students... permitted uses, if any') while supporting 'responsible experimentation'.

units.why: Opens with the university's stance that it 'supports responsible experimentation and use', a default welcoming AI with conditions; P02 (permit by default).
units.anchor: The University supports responsible experimentation and use of AI tools
units.fit_note: Support is for responsible experimentation, with listed cautions.

units.why: Defines generative AI to set what the guidance covers, P61.
units.anchor: Generative AI goes beyond traditional AI systems by creating new data

units.why: Warns that data entered into AI tools may be reused in unintended ways, a privacy and data concern, P50.
units.anchor: may be used in ways you did not intend or anticipate

units.why: States the guidelines apply existing university policy rather than creating new policy, P77 (comply with existing policy).
units.anchor: not new University policy; rather, they leverage existing University policies
units.fit_note: Describes the guideline's status; it does not tell users to comply.

units.why: Commits to monitoring and updating the guidelines with community feedback, P54.
units.anchor: monitor developments and incorporate feedback from the university community

units.why: A direct prohibition on entering sensitive or confidential data into AI tools not authorized by the university; privacy rule and preference for approved tools, P50.
units.anchor: Do not enter sensitive or confidential information, including non-public research data, into AI tools

units.why: Users own what they produce or publish even if AI-generated, P29.
units.anchor: You are responsible for any content you produce or publish, including AI-generated content

units.why: Warns that AI output can be wrong or fabricated, P31. Copyright and confidential content risks in the same sentence are secondary to the accuracy warning.
units.anchor: AI-generated content can be inaccurate, misleading, or entirely fabricated

units.why: Instructs users to review AI output before sharing, i.e. verify it, P31.
units.anchor: Review your AI-generated content before publication or sharing

units.why: In a list of AI-generated content for which users are responsible, it names academic work completed in a way the instructor does not allow; the instructor sets the limits, P04. The list's grammar is loose, so I treat this only as informing.
units.anchor: completion of academic work in a manner not allowed by the instructor
units.fit_note: Appears as a list example, not a freestanding rule.

units.why: Students' AI use must follow existing academic integrity requirements in university policies and codes, P77.
units.anchor: Students’ use of AI tools must adhere to university requirements regarding academic integrity

units.why: Faculty should tell students what AI use is permitted ('if any'), P09 (state expectations).
units.anchor: Faculty should be clear with students in their courses regarding permitted uses

units.why: Students are encouraged to ask when unsure about permitted uses, P10.
units.anchor: encouraged to ask their instructors for clarification about permitted uses

units.why: Faculty and staff acquiring AI tools must follow university procurement rules, which review tools for compliance, privacy and security, P65.
units.anchor: must adhere to university policies and standards regarding the acquisition of new IT products

units.why: Gives the reason for the procurement rule: processes ensure tools have compliance, privacy and security protections; same review function as P65.
units.anchor: processes ensure that IT products and services have sufficient compliance, privacy, and security protections

notes: No school or computing-unit policy found; course layer deferred. All four documents delegate: Texas State states it has no AI policy and leaves rules to instructors. The Information Security Office page says its guidelines are not new policy. Coder B.
